```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = identical(Sys.getenv("RCEATTLE_EVAL_VIGNETTES"), "true"),
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5
)
```

How to check a fitted model, using the 2022 Northern Rockfish assessment as the
example:

- **convergence diagnostics**: attached automatically to every fit made with `estimateMode` `"Estimate"` or `"Hindcast"`
- **S3 methods**: `residuals()`, `logLik()`, and the like
- **fit plots**: compare predicted to observed data
- **one-step-ahead (OSA) and process residuals**: goodness-of-fit tests for the observation and process models
- **retrospective analysis**: peel off recent years to detect systematic bias
- **jitter testing**: perturb starting values to check the optimizer found a global minimum
- **self-testing** (simulation–estimation): check the model recovers its own estimates from simulated data
- **likelihood profiling**: check how informative the data are about a given parameter

Printing any of them opens with one line (the object, an overall status, and a
verdict) before the detail:

```
<Rceattle convergence>  status: OK
  all checks OK

<Rceattle OSA diagnostics>  status: WARN
  7 of 7 source(s) outside a null interval; overall SDNR 1.82 (0.91-1.09)
          source  fleet  n     sdnr   null
  [WARN]  index      4     36  2.52   0.77-1.23
  ...

<Rceattle retrospective>  status: WARN
  4 peel(s); 3 of 12 terminal Mohn's rho outside +/-0.2
          quantity  N     Pollock  Cod      Arrowtooth flounder
  [WARN]  R            3  0.511    0.283    -0.221

<Rceattle jitter>  status: OK
  4 of 4 start(s) reached the best optimum (within 0.01)

<Rceattle self-test>  status: NOTE
  47 of 50 simulation(s) converged
          convergence  n
  [OK  ]  OK           41
  [NOTE]  NOTE          6
  observations redrawn, processes held at their fitted values: the spread is a lower bound

<Rceattle profile>  status: WARN
  sigmaR over 29 grid point(s); all converged
  minimum -log L : 1274.8831  at slot_1 = 1.5
  within 1.92 of the minimum : 1.3 to >=1.5
  the minimum is at a grid edge (slot_1), so the grid does not bracket it -- widen `values`
```

The severity is `OK`, `NOTE`, `WARN` or `FAIL`, and the overall status is the
worst present. Only the printing gives a verdict: each object is a data frame or
list (`retro$mohns`, `jit$nll`, `diag$sdnr`, `prof$grid$slot_1`,
`sims[["Sim_1"]]`), and `c(sims, list(fit))` gives a plain list of fits to plot.

Four print methods take a threshold:

- `print(retro, band = )`: Mohn's rho threshold. The default `0.2` is the rule
  of thumb below; Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015) give asymmetric,
  life-history-dependent alternatives (−0.15 to 0.20 long-lived, −0.22 to 0.30
  short-lived).
- `print(jit, tol = )`: how close an objective must be to count as having
  reached the same optimum.
- `print(sims, rate = )`: the fraction of simulations that must converge before
  a self-test counts as clean.
- `print(prof, cutoff = )`: bounds the reported interval; the default 1.92 is
  the 95% profile-likelihood cutoff for one parameter, half the 0.95 quantile of
  a chi-square on one degree of freedom.

A self-test's header gives the convergence rate against `nsim` and its last
line says what generated the replicates (see the self-test section). A profile
whose minimum sits at the first or last grid value has run out of grid; it plots
as an ordinary curve, so the print says so and asks for a wider `values`.

## Setup and plotting data

```{r}
library(Rceattle)

# Fit a single-species model for the 2022 Northern Rockfish assessment.
data("NorthernRockfish2022")
nrdata <- NorthernRockfish2022
nrdata$fleet_control$Proj_F_proportion <- 1
plot_data(nrdata)
```

Fit the model.
```{r}
model_1 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(
  data_list = nrdata,
  estimateMode = 0,  # Estimate
  initMode = 1,      # Assume unfished equilibrium
  M1Fun = build_M1(
    updateM1 = TRUE,
    M1_model = 1,
    M1_use_prior = TRUE,
    M_prior = 0.06,
    M_prior_sd = 0.05),
  fit_control = fit_control(phase = TRUE, verbose = 0)
)
summary(model_1)
```

## S3 Methods

```{r}
summary(model_1)              # same compact summary
coef(model_1)                 # estimated fixed-effect parameters
logLik(model_1)               # logLik with df attribute (AIC works)
AIC(model_1)
vcov(model_1)                 # fixed-effect covariance from sdreport
residuals(model_1)                    # response residuals, all data sources
residuals(model_1, type = "pearson")  # Pearson residuals (glm-style `type`)
as.data.frame(model_1)
```


## Convergence diagnostics

After optimization, `fit_mod()` runs a battery of convergence checks and attaches
them as `model$convergence`; `status` is the worst `severity` present. `WARN`
and `FAIL` checks are reported by `message()` during the fit, and `print(model)` shows the
overall status. A non-converged fit is still returned, never an error, so you
decide whether to trust it.

```{r}
model_1$convergence            # overall status + any non-OK checks
print(model_1$convergence, all = TRUE)   # show every check, including OK ones
```

Re-run the battery on any fit with `convergence_diagnostics()`:

```{r}
convergence_diagnostics(model_1)
```

The checks cover:

- **`max_gradient`**: maximum absolute marginal gradient and the parameter
  holding it (`WARN` > 1e-3, `FAIL` > 1). With an `sdreport` of the same
  parameters, the message also gives the distance to the optimum in standard
  errors (largest in `$data$newton_step_se`, signed vector in
  `$data$step_se`), which unlike the raw gradient is comparable across log,
  logit and natural-scale parameters: 0.02 means finishing the optimization
  would move no estimate by more than 2% of its standard error. The severity is
  read on the gradient.
- **`pdHess`**: whether the Hessian is positive definite (`FAIL` if not).
- **`sdreport_failed`**: `FAIL` when an `sdreport` was requested but the
  Hessian could not be inverted.
- **`hessian_not_run`**: `NOTE` when the fit was made with `getsd = FALSE`, so
  `pdHess`, `hessian_conditioning`, `sdreport_failed` and `estimability` never
  ran; refit with `getsd = TRUE` before reading the status as convergence.
- **`zero_n_penalty`**: the "Zero n-at-age penalty" likelihood row is non-zero
  for a species: its numbers-at-age, Ricker intercept or (under an identity-link
  recruitment linkage) recruitment sat on the 0.001 floor, so the fit is of a
  floored model rather than the one specified. `WARN` when the root-sum-square
  excursion is under 1 (a thousand fish), `FAIL` above.
- **`hessian_conditioning`**: how much better the data pin down some parameter
  combinations than others: the condition number of the correlation matrix of
  the estimates (`WARN` above 1e6, `FAIL` above 1e10), the multi-parameter
  version of a 0.999 pairwise correlation. On a fishery it usually means F
  traded against selectivity. Its square root is a ratio of standard errors
  on the standardized scale (each parameter divided by its own standard
  error): 13,634 means the least-determined
  combination is 13,634 times more uncertain than the best-determined one. The
  covariance condition number, which is not scale-invariant, is reported as
  `covariance_condition_number`.
- **`parameters_on_bounds`**: parameters that sit on a configured
  `build_bounds()` limit (often unidentified or mis-scaled). `WARN`: the edge of
  the plausible range is still a well-posed optimum.
- **`parameters_outside_bounds`**: parameters past one, a `FAIL`. `nlminb`
  respects the bounds but the Newton refinement `fit_control(newtonsteps)` asks
  for afterwards does not; refit with `newtonsteps = 0`, the default.
- **`variance_collapse`**: a deviation standard deviation estimated to zero
  (`WARN` below 1e-3): a process configured as time-varying has fitted as
  time-invariant. Covers the recruitment, selectivity, catchability, M1 and
  linkage random-effect standard deviations. `WARN` rather than `FAIL` because a
  variance at the boundary is a well-posed optimum; it can occur with a clean
  gradient.
- **`stock_recruit`**: whether the fitted curve is one the data informed. In a
  single-species model it is read against the replacement line through
  steepness. Under predation steepness does not exist (it needs spawning biomass
  per recruit), so the curve is read over the observed SSB range instead: `WARN`
  when it is flat there (recruitment independent of SSB), linear (no density
  dependence), when a Ricker peaks below the lowest observed SSB, when log alpha
  or log beta sits at its +/-30 bound, or when a log-scale standard error exceeds
  10. A curve held at its inputs is a `NOTE`.
- **`exponential_q_near_one`**: `WARN` for a fleet with an `exponential`
  catchability linkage whose fitted catchability is within 0.1% of 1. That link
  multiplies `log q`, so at `q = 1` the covariate moves the index by nothing
  whatever the coefficient is, and the coefficient is unidentified.
- **`phasing`**: phases that ended with a high gradient, localizing which
  parameter block is hard to fit.
- **`estimability`**: surfaces `TMBhelper::check_estimability` when it ran.

### Naming the parameter, not just the block

`max_gradient`, `estimability`, the two bounds checks and `hessian_conditioning`
name the flagged element by fleet, sex, age, bin and year, from
`parameter_index()`, not just its parameter block (`sel_coff_dev`, say), and
follow the block name with the quantity it estimates, from
[`parameter_dictionary()`]:

```
  [WARN] max_gradient     Maximum absolute marginal gradient = 0.00222 on log_M1 (M1): Pollock, age 1.
  [WARN] hessian_conditioning Condition number = 2.4e+06: standard errors span 1.5e+03x across parameter combinations; loads on: log_F (F): 67% + rec_dev (recruitment deviations): 26%.
  log_F (F)                        Hake_fishery, 38 years in 1980-2021  (38 of 44 parameters; 67% of the direction)
  rec_dev (recruitment deviations) 24 years in 1981-2013  (24 of 44 parameters; 26% of the direction)
```

A scattered set of years or ages is counted against its span ("38 years in
1980-2021"); a consecutive run prints as a range. The count in parentheses is
how many of the block's parameters carry 90% of its loading.

`max_gradient`, `estimability` and the two bounds checks are captured from the
hindcast optimization; `hessian_conditioning` reads the `sdreport`, which under
an estimating HCR belongs to the projection fit and holds only `log_Ftarget` /
`log_Flimit`. A check prints block names alone when the index does not describe
the vector it is about to label.

`parameter_index()` itself describes `fit$obj`, which under any HCR but
`"NoFishing"` is that projection object. Pass a fit run with
`estimateMode = "Hindcast"` to browse the hindcast parameters directly.

## Fit plots

### Composition data

`plot_comp()` draws composition Pearson-residual bubbles and overlays the
observed (shaded area) and predicted (line) age or length compositions for every
fleet, both annually and aggregated across years. Joint-sex data are drawn on a
single bin axis with females above and males below zero.

```{r}
plot_comp(model_1)
```

### Survey indices

`plot_index()` shows observed vs. predicted survey biomass; pass `log = TRUE` for the log scale. The predicted line is the median of the fitted observation distribution, so about half the observations should fall below it. `plot_index_residual()` plots the Pearson residual (observed minus predicted, standardized by the sd the row was fitted with), a first check for time trends or heteroscedasticity. A positive residual means the survey saw more than the model predicted. These return `ggplot` objects.

```{r}
plot_index(model_1)
plot_index(model_1, log = TRUE)
plot_index_residual(model_1)
```

`plot_catchability()` draws the realized catchability the model scaled each survey by, faceted by fleet, so one figure covers an estimated or fixed mean, annual deviations under `Time_varying_q`, an environmental regression, a `q` linkage such as `rw(1 | Year)`, and the closed-form `"Analytical"` value. A time-invariant `q` draws a flat line. Hindcast years only; the model does not project catchability.

```{r}
plot_catchability(model_1)
plot_catchability(model_1, log = TRUE)
```

### Catch

```{r}
plot_catch(model_1)
```

## One-step-ahead (OSA) residuals

Pearson residuals on composition data are *not* standard normal even when the
model is correct: the age/length bins are correlated (more fish in one bin means
fewer in another), and random effects induce correlation across years. (They are
standardized by the variance the fleet's own likelihood assumes, so composition
weighting or Dirichlet-multinomial overdispersion does not inflate them.)
One-step-ahead (OSA) residuals remove both problems. Each observation is
residualized conditional on the observations added before it, integrating out
the random effects, so under a correctly specified model the residuals are iid
standard normal (Thygesen et al. 2017; Trijoulet et al. 2023).

`osa_residuals()` computes them *post hoc* for any combination of the fitted data
types: survey indices (`"index"`), fishery catch (`"catch"`), age/length
composition (`"comp"`), conditional age-at-length (`"caal"`), predator diet
(`"diet"`), and, where a linkage holds an observed state-space covariate, the
covariate observation itself (`"ecov"`). Composition data use the conditional
binomial / beta-binomial decomposition of Trijoulet et al. (2023), using code
adapted from WHAM (Stock and Miller 2021). OSA re-optimizes the random effects for
each observation, so it is expensive; run it on a converged fit
(`estimateMode < 3`). A requested source the model has no observations for is
skipped (the call errors only if *none* of them have any). `"diet"` is not in
the default set (multispecies only, and can be slow); pass `source = "all"` to
include it. It needs a *predicted* diet, which means `msmMode > 0` **and**
estimated suitability (`suitMode` 2, 4 or 6); under empirical suitability the
diet diagnostics refuse rather than report every observation as a complete
misfit.

```{r osa}
# Aggregate (catch + index) residuals
osa <- osa_residuals(model_1, source = c("index", "catch"))
head(osa)

# Statistical diagnostics (Stewart & Monnahan 2025): SDNR and lower/upper tail
# statistics, each with the interval expected under the standard-normal null.
osa_diagnostics(osa)

# Q-Q plot (with SDNR / tail annotation) + residual-by-year
plot(osa)

# residuals() also exposes them in the common residual schema (`source` selects
# the data, like `type` in stats::residuals.glm()):
residuals(model_1, type = "osa", source = c("index", "catch"))

# Composition OSA residuals, no special fit required
plot_comp(model_1, residual_type = "osa")              # Q-Q + signed bubbles
residuals(model_1, type = "osa", source = "comp")
```

A triangle marks an outlier. On the OSA panel the cut is `qnorm(1 - 0.05 / (2 n))`
for the panel's `n` residuals, so under the model a panel shows 0.05 triangles on
average whatever its size. The Pearson panel keeps `|resid| > 3`: those residuals
are sum-constrained and overdispersed, not N(0, 1).

### Choosing the one-step-ahead method

`method` selects how the conditional distribution is read. The default,
`"oneStepGaussianOffMode"` (WHAM's and SAM's), approximates it as Gaussian.
`method = "cdf"` asks the model for the conditional CDF and returns
`qnorm(F(x))`: a binomial for a composition bin (defined at fractional counts),
`pnorm` for the aggregate series. On a fixed-effect model nothing is
approximated; with random effects see below.

The two disagree on composition data. Scored by simulating from a fitted model
and residualizing at the generating parameters, where the right answer is
exactly standard normal (BS2017SS, 20 replicates of 4538 composition bins):

| method | mean | sd | lag-1 acf within a composition | KS rejects |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `oneStepGaussianOffMode` | +0.103 | 0.918 | +0.060 | every replicate |
| `cdf`, `discrete = FALSE` | +0.610 | 1.262 | +0.434 | every replicate |
| `cdf`, `discrete = TRUE` | −0.007 | 0.995 | +0.001 | none |

The null standard error on the autocorrelation is 0.015, so only the last row is
consistent with iid standard normal residuals. A composition bin holds a count,
so its conditional CDF is a step function; the randomized quantile residual
`qnorm(F(x) − U f(x))` (Dunn and Smyth 1996, as Trijoulet et al. 2023
prescribe) removes the step, which is why `discrete` defaults to `TRUE` under
`"cdf"`. On the aggregate index and catch series, which really are Gaussian, all
three agree to 5e-5 wherever the 8.04 ceiling below does not bind.

The step is the **model's**, not the data's: the likelihood reads counts as
`proportion × Sample_size`, so on a fleet whose sample size has been tuned they
are not whole fish, and a heavily down-weighted fleet is residualized against a
multinomial it was never sampled from.

```{r osa-cdf}
osa_cdf <- osa_residuals(model_1, source = c("index", "comp"), method = "cdf")
osa_diagnostics(osa_cdf)
```

Three things to know before switching:

* **`predicted` is `NA` on every row**: the method forms no conditional mean.
  Fitted values are in `model_1$quantities` and in
  `residuals(model_1, type = "pearson")`. (`sd` is `NA` under the default
  method as well; only `method = "oneStepGaussian"` returns one.)
* **A Dirichlet-multinomial fleet cannot use it.** Its beta-binomial
  conditional has no closed-form CDF and cannot be summed at a fractional
  count. Those fleets are residualized with `"oneStepGaussianOffMode"`,
  announced in a message and recorded in the object's `method` attribute, and
  their `predicted` is blanked too.
* **`|residual|` is censored at 8.04, in both directions**: double precision
  sets the upper end, and the lower is matched so that a one-sided ceiling does
  not look like skewness. `osa_diagnostics()` computes SDNR and the tail
  statistics on the censored values, so the censoring bites hardest on a short
  series where one observation holds the statistic. `osa_residuals()` warns
  when any residual sits there. On a 12-year survey with one observation
  multiplied by 200:

  | method | min | max | non-finite | SDNR |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | `oneStepGaussianOffMode` | −11.77 | 0.19 | 1 | `NA` |
  | `oneStepGaussian` | −11.77 | 38.98 | 0 | 12.89 |
  | `oneStepGeneric` | −3.95 | 3.33 | 0 | 2.21 |
  | `cdf` | −8.04 | 8.04 | 0 | 4.59 |

  Only `"oneStepGaussian"` reports the uncensored value here: the package
  default returns `NaN` on that row, so its SDNR is unusable, and
  `"oneStepGeneric"` compresses the outlier harder than the ceiling does. The
  default's failure is magnitude-dependent (at a ×20 outlier it is finite and
  matches `"oneStepGaussian"`), so use `"oneStepGaussian"` itself, on the fleet
  in question: it costs an `nlminb` per observation.

### With random effects, the choice reverses for the aggregate series

`"cdf"` is exact only on a fixed-effect model: with random effects its Laplace
integration over the latent states is approximate, while for a Gaussian
observation the Gaussian methods are exact. Measured against the exact Kalman
innovations of a linear-Gaussian state space model, as the latent state becomes
more informative relative to the observation:

| latent/observation sd | `fullGaussian` | `oneStepGaussian` | `cdf` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.56 | 4e-16 | 3e-14 | 7e-04 |
| 1.12 | 1e-15 | 4e-14 | 6e-03 |
| 2.24 | 1e-15 | 3e-14 | 4e-02 |

That does not transfer wholesale: the Gaussian methods are exact when the
one-step-ahead *predictive* is Gaussian, which needs the model to be linear in
the random effects, and Rceattle's index and catch are `exp()` of cumulated log
recruitment deviations pushed through the population dynamics. On a
17-deviation fixture `fullGaussian` and `oneStepGaussian`, which cannot differ
for a Gaussian conditional, differ by 0.091 on both index and catch, while
`"cdf"` differs from `oneStepGaussian` by 0.017 on index. **No method is exact
for index or catch under random effects.**

**`"ecov"` is the exception, and there a Gaussian method is right.** Its
conditional (a Gaussian measurement of an AR1 latent) genuinely is
linear-Gaussian: the two Gaussian methods agree to 4e-14 on the QAR1 fixture,
while `"cdf"` sits 0.139 away, about a quarter of the residual sd.

The choice does not reverse for compositions, whose discrete, skewed
conditional the Gaussian methods get wrong by much more. Simulating from a
22-random-effect model with the recruitment deviations redrawn and
residualizing at the generating parameters (1680 residuals, 120 replicates):

| method | mean | sd | KS rejects |
|---|---|---|---|
| `oneStepGaussianOffMode` | +0.513 | 0.404 | 120 of 120 |
| `cdf`, `discrete = TRUE` | +0.006 | 1.002 | 6 of 120 (the nominal 5%) |

What limits `"cdf"` on compositions is the depth of the conditioning rather than
the random effects themselves. On `BS2017SS` with `random_rec = TRUE` (159 random
effects, 4538 composition bins) it returns 1879 non-finite residuals, against 0
for `"oneStepGaussianOffMode"` on the same fit, and takes hours; the same rows
residualized on their own come back clean. Try it, read the warning it issues,
and where the residuals come back non-finite in bulk fall back to a Gaussian
method for that source, remembering that its composition residuals are the
under-dispersed ones in the comparison above. Within one call every source uses
`method`, apart from the automatic Dirichlet-multinomial, `discrete = TRUE` and
`TruncatedNormal` overrides; `discrete` applies only to composition sources.
(SAM's authors split the method by data type, across two packages:
`stockassessment::residuals.sam()` takes `oneStepPredict()`'s
`"oneStepGaussianOffMode"` default with `discrete = FALSE`, while
`compResidual::resMulti()`, the implementation Trijoulet et al. (2023) cite,
hardcodes `method = "cdf", discrete = TRUE`.)

For every method, `Estimate_index_sd = "Analytical"`,
`Estimate_catch_sd = "Analytical"` and the analytical `Catchability` forms
concentrate their parameter out using **all** the observations, including the
one being residualized, so the residuals are approximate, by an amount that
shrinks as the series lengthens.

### Fleets with tail accumulation

Where a fleet folds its composition tails into a boundary bin
(`Comp_accum_young` / `Comp_accum_old`), both the OSA and the Pearson residuals
describe the bins the likelihood actually fit, not the raw bins in `comp_data`.
A fleet on 10 ages with `Comp_accum_young = 3` reports bins 3 to 10: bin 3 holds
ages 1 to 3 combined, and the `accumulated` column (`Accumulated` from
`residuals()`) marks it. The one-step-ahead decomposition drops each
composition's last bin, fixed by the sum-to-sample-size constraint, so under an
*old*-tail accumulation the upper boundary bin appears in the Pearson residuals
and not in the OSA residuals.

Following Stewart and Monnahan (2025), a practical workflow is:

1. **Inspect the aggregate fit** (`plot_comp(model_1)`, pooled across the fitted
   hindcast years): systematic lack of fit points to structural
   misspecification (e.g. the wrong selectivity shape). The interval holds 95%
   of the data the model predicts, not a confidence interval on the mean, so
   observations outside it are the ones to explain. The panel gives the input
   sample size, the effective sample size the likelihood assumed
   (`ESS (likelihood)`), and the one this fit's residuals imply
   (`ESS (McAllister-Ianelli)`); the gap between the last two is the
   reweighting decision.
2. **Compare the SDNR** to its null interval (from `osa_diagnostics()`): a value
   outside the interval flags over- or under-dispersion, often a data-weighting
   or effective-sample-size issue.
3. **Compare the lower/upper tail statistics** to their null intervals, to
   localize departures to the tails. They are order statistics: `lower_r` /
   `upper_r` name which one and `lower_p` / `upper_p` its nominal probability
   (near but not exactly 2.5%), against the exact `Beta(r, n - r + 1)` null.
   `osa_diagnostics()` does not simulate, so its `nsim` / `seed` arguments are
   ignored.
4. **Inspect Pearson bubble plots** (`plot_comp(model_1)`, the default): the
   sign pattern across age/year can show *where* lack of fit occurs; Stewart and
   Monnahan recommend keeping these alongside OSA residuals.
5. **Revise the model or data weighting** where misspecification is found, using
   this together with the other diagnostics rather than as an accept/reject test.

When the diagnosis is a weighting problem rather than a structural one,
`reweight_comps()` runs the McAllister-Ianelli (1997) tuning loop, refitting the
model as it was fitted and updating each fleet's `Comp_weights` until the
implied weights settle.

```{r}
tuned <- reweight_comps(model_1, n_iter = 10, tol = 0.01)
tuned$reweight$history    # weight per fleet, per iteration
```

Restrict it with `fleets =`, giving `Fleet_code` values or names matching
`fleet_control$Fleet_name`, not a mix (R coerces `c(1, "Survey")` to character).

```{r}
tuned <- reweight_comps(model_1, fleets = c("Bottom_trawl", "Fishery"))
```

Only multinomial fleets are tuned: a Dirichlet-multinomial fleet estimates its
own weight inside the likelihood, so those fleets are named and skipped.

The alternatives are Francis (2011) reweighting, applied by hand, and estimating
the weights directly with a Dirichlet-multinomial likelihood (Thorson et al.
2017; `Comp_distribution = "DirichletMultinomial"`), with no iteration. Under
that likelihood `Comp_weights` is the **log** of the starting weight, so the model
default of `1` is a starting weight of *e*, and a weight of 1 is written `0`.

Under `discrete = TRUE` (the default only for `method = "cdf"`), composition
residuals are randomized quantile residuals, so stochastic; `osa_residuals()`
takes a `seed` for reproducibility.

### Process residuals

`process_residuals()` checks the *process* model: it standardizes the
random-effect deviations (recruitment, initial abundance, catchability) against
their process prior, drawing once from the joint posterior (SAM's `procres`;
Nielsen and Berg 2014). Under a correct process model these too are
approximately iid standard normal.

```{r procres}
pr <- process_residuals(model_1, process = "recruitment")
osa_diagnostics(pr)
plot(pr)

# residuals() exposes them too:
residuals(model_1, type = "process")
```

## Retrospective analysis

A retrospective analysis removes the most recent years of data one peel at a time and re-fits the model. Mohn's rho (Mohn 1999), averaged over peels as in Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015), summarizes how the terminal estimates shift across peels; for SSB, a rho outside ±0.2 generally signals a problem worth investigating.

```{r}
model_1_retro <- retrospective(model_1, peels = 5)

# Mohn's rho for each quantity
model_1_retro$mohns

# Plot historical trajectories across peels
plot_biomass(model_1_retro$Rceattle_list)

# Include the projection period to see how the forecast changes
plot_biomass(model_1_retro$Rceattle_list, incl_proj = TRUE)
```

Each peel holds its own terminal year as `data_list$endyr`, so the first plot draws every peel only as far as it was fit. `retrospective()` returns:

| Element | Description |
|---|---|
| `Rceattle_list` | the fitted peels, deepest first, then the full run, each named for its terminal year (`Year_2017`, …, `Year_2022`) |
| `mohns` | Mohn's rho (mean relative error) by `Object` (`"biomass"`, `"ssb"`, `"R"`, `"F_spp"`) and `Forecast year` (0 = terminal-year bias; 1 to `nyrs_forecast`, default 3, = forecast skill), with `N` the peels used in that row and one column per species |
| `peels_requested` | the `peels` asked for |

A peel is refitted as a model ending at its terminal year. The years it dropped are then its retrospective forecast: F is fitted to the observed catch, with those years' survey and composition data withheld, and so is their `env_data`, except the columns `?retrospective` lists. The forecast years are `endyr_peel + seq_len(endyr_full - endyr_peel)`, where `endyr_peel` is the peel's terminal year and `endyr_full` the unpeeled one; the harvest control rule takes over after `endyr_full`, through `projyr`, and `incl_proj = TRUE` plots both. A series known ahead, such as a climate projection, goes in `projected_env_data_known = "<column>"` so the peels keep it, and `rescale = "<column>"` standardizes a covariate on each peel's retained years.

`print(model_1_retro)` counts the peels that were dropped or flagged:

- A peel whose hindcast did not converge is dropped with a warning (under `getsd = TRUE`, so is one whose hindcast Hessian is not positive definite), so index `Rceattle_list` by name rather than position. If no peel converges, Mohn's rho is `NaN` and the call warns.
- A peel whose forecast refit did not fit F to the peeled catch is kept with no warning, but only in the `$mohns` rows with `Forecast year` 0; `attr(peel, "forecast_refit_error")` gives the reason. `plot_biomass()` and the other `plot_timeseries()` wrappers warn when they draw that peel's forecast years; `plot_catch()`, the other plotters and `as.data.frame()` do not.
- Under `getsd = TRUE` (the default when the input model has standard errors), a peel whose standard-error rebuild fails after its forecast refit is kept with no warning, but `plot_biomass()`, `as.data.frame()` and `vcov()` read none from it, since `peel$sdrep` may then hold no valid standard errors; `attr(peel, "sd_report_error")` gives the reason.

`?retrospective` covers the standard-error bands, how a peel treats each `env_data` column, and `rescale`.

## Jitter testing

Jitter testing re-fits the model from many randomly perturbed starting values and checks whether the optimizer keeps returning the same minimum negative log-likelihood (NLL); a spread of NLL values points to multiple local minima. Each start re-fits under the fit's own map (which parameters are estimated and which are fixed), so a parameter you fixed keeps its value, and the NLL values compare with the fit's unless it used `fit_mod(bounds = )`. A projection-only fit (`estimateMode = "Projection"`) re-fits under the default map from `build_map()`, so nothing fixed in its map carries over and its NLL values do not compare; see `?jitter`.

```{r}
jitters <- jitter(model_1, njitter = 10, phase = TRUE)  # default njitter = 50

# Histogram of NLL differences relative to the best run
hist(log(jitters$nll - min(jitters$nll)),
     main = "Jitter NLL spread (log scale)",
     xlab = "log(NLL - min NLL)")

# Overlay biomass trajectories, tight overlap indicates a stable optimum
plot_biomass(jitters$Rceattle_list)

# Number of runs that converged
length(jitters$Rceattle_list)
```

Non-converging runs are dropped from `Rceattle_list` and reported in a message, so if `length(jitters$Rceattle_list)` is well below `njitter`, convergence is fragile; the dropped starts are the ones that wandered off, so the successes alone understate the spread. A run is dropped when its maximum absolute gradient exceeds 1 (the `FAIL` threshold in `convergence_diagnostics()`) or when a requested `sdreport` failed or gave `pdHess = FALSE`.

`retrospective()` and `jitter()` both fit peels / starts in parallel by default, on `parallel::detectCores() - 6` cores (2 under `R CMD check`); pass `cores = 1` to run them sequentially.

## Self-test (simulation–estimation)

`self_test()` simulates `nsim` datasets from a fitted model (holding its estimated parameters fixed) and re-fits the model to each. If the refit estimates cluster around the values used to simulate them, the model can at least recover its own estimates from data it generated; persistent bias or a wide spread in a quantity means the data are not informative about it. Each simulation re-fits under the fit's own map, so a parameter you fixed keeps its value.

```{r}
sims <- self_test(model_1, nsim = 10)            # default nsim = 50

# Number of simulations that converged (non-converged runs are dropped)
length(sims)

# Overlay biomass / SSB trajectories across simulations, the original fit's
# trajectory should sit inside the spread of the refits.
plot_biomass(c(list(model_1), sims), model_names = c("fit", names(sims)))
plot_ssb(c(list(model_1), sims),     model_names = c("fit", names(sims)))
```

Each simulation uses `seed + i` as its RNG seed, so results are reproducible whether or not `cores > 1`. Set `simulate = FALSE` to refit against the model's *expected* values (no observation error), to confirm that the estimator returns the generating parameters in the noise-free limit. `cores` behaves as in `retrospective()` and `jitter()`.

Every refit starts from the fitted model's *starting* values, not its estimates, and `phase` defaults to whatever the input model was fit with; pass `phase = TRUE` if you fit the model some other way and the refits are being dropped. `start = "estimated"` starts from the fitted estimates instead: much faster, but the optimizer then begins inside the basin containing the generating values, so recovery is close to guaranteed by construction; read it as optimistic.

When reading the result:

- **Non-converged refits are dropped** (reported in a message) *because* they behaved badly, so any spread or bias computed over the rest (including `compare_sim()`'s CV) understates the truth.
- **By default only the observations are redrawn**: every replicate shares the operating model's single realization of recruitment and mortality, so the spread is observation error alone, a lower bound on estimation uncertainty in SSB and recruitment, not comparable to the model's own uncertainty bands.
- **Watch for a truncation warning on a natural-scale index.** A fleet with `Index_distribution = "Normal"`, `"MVN"` or `"MVNORM"` is drawn on the natural scale with an absolute sd, so a draw can come out negative, which `data_check()` rejects. Those draws are redrawn, sampling the fleet from a normal *truncated at zero* rather than the untruncated normal the likelihood maximises. Occasional truncation is harmless; a lot is not. `sim_mod()` warns above 2% truncation: for a `Normal` fleet, when any row puts more than 2% of its probability at or below zero, `Phi(-mu/sd)`, read off the fit, so it does not vary between replicates; for an `MVN`/`MVNORM` fleet, whenever that replicate rejected a whole-vector draw, so it varies between replicates.

The fix for a `Normal` fleet is `Index_distribution = "TruncatedNormal"`, which fits the truncated density, renormalized by `log Φ(µ/σ)` over `(0, ∞)`, and draws from it by inverse CDF, so draw and likelihood agree and no draw is rejected. `"Normal"` reproduces the AMAK `avo_like` / `cpue_like` term for term, which is what an ADMB bridge compares against; use it there and `"TruncatedNormal"` elsewhere (`data_check()` refuses `"TruncatedNormal"` with `Catchability = "Analytical"`). `MVN`/`MVNORM` have no truncated option, so the gap stays. Either way, an absolute sd that large relative to the index means the natural-scale normal was a poor observation model to begin with.

`"TruncatedNormal"` OSA residuals need nothing from you. The Gaussian methods (including the default `oneStepGaussianOffMode`) would return the untruncated `(obs - µ)/σ`, so `osa_residuals()` overrides `method` for those rows only, integrating the truncated density to give `qnorm(F(x))`; under `method = "cdf"` the model supplies the truncated `F` in closed form. The correction is the size of the truncated mass: on a fleet predicting 100 with an absolute sd of 150, an observation exactly at the prediction moves from a residual of 0 to −0.44.

### Redrawing process error

The default `process = FALSE` asks whether the estimator recovers its own parameters from new observations; naming a process redraws that process too, and asks whether it recovers something it was not shown.

```{r}
# Recruitment deviations redrawn as well as the observations
sims <- self_test(model_1, nsim = 10, process = "recruitment")

# "dynamics" covers recruitment, M and growth; "observation" covers
# catchability and selectivity; TRUE covers everything.
sims <- self_test(model_1, nsim = 10, process = "dynamics")
```

Recruitment covers the initial age structure as well as the hindcast deviations, since the initial numbers-at-age are recruitment from before `styr`. Natural mortality covers the `M1_re` random effects, and growth, catchability and selectivity are redrawn wherever they are written as a random linkage (see `vignette("environmental-linkages-and-priors")`). A process the model gives no distribution to (asking for M when `M1_re = 0`, say) is left alone and reported in a warning. Redrawing a deviation the fit's map fixes also warns, because the refit holds it fixed and cannot recover the draw.

Recruitment has one such case. Under `srr_fun = 0` with `srr_pred_fun > 0` (the AMAK/Ianelli configuration, where recruitment is estimated annually and the stock-recruit curve is fitted as a *penalty* on those same deviations) the deviations are scored by two densities at once, which do not compose into a distribution to draw from: the penalty couples them to the stock-recruit parameters, which are estimated too, so drawing from either term alone would test recovery against a process the model does not assume. The deviations are not redrawn and `sim_mod()` says why; a random linkage on a recruitment parameter is a separate latent and is still drawn. Set `srr_fun` to the stock-recruit function itself to redraw the deviations.

The fitted deviations are not what generated the data; the values that *did* are attached to each replicate, each with a mask of the cells the draw touched:

```{r}
truth <- attr(sims, "process_sim")[["Sim_1"]]
rec   <- truth$rec_dev[truth$rec_dev_drawn]
```

Compare estimates against those, not against the operating model, and only over the mask: the process draws cover the hindcast only, and `beta_linkage_re` spans every random linkage whether or not its process was asked for. For the same reason `compare_sim()`, which compares against the operating model, is not valid for `process`-drawn replicates.

Read a self-test that redraws M as a test of deviation recovery rather than of variance recovery. On `BS2017SS` with a year-varying M random effect, refits recover the simulated deviations (correlation around 0.5, positive in every replicate) but their standard deviation roughly 70% low, collapsing to zero in a third of replicates: a year-varying M is weakly informed, since it trades off against selectivity and catchability.

When the returned list is shorter than `nsim`, `debug = TRUE` returns *every* simulation, so the failures can be read directly:

```{r}
sims <- self_test(model_1, nsim = 10, debug = TRUE)

failed <- names(which(!attr(sims, "converged")))
sims[[failed[1]]]$convergence          # which check failed, and on which parameter
```

## Likelihood profile

`profile()` re-fits the model across a grid of fixed values for a chosen parameter and returns the NLL surface. A flat profile means the data say little about the parameter; a minimum away from the MLE means the fit has not truly settled there.

Specify the parameter with a natural-scale alias, which takes natural-scale
values directly: `"sigmaR"` (the standard deviation of the log-scale
recruitment deviations, not a CV of recruitment in thousands of fish), `"M1"`
(natural mortality), or the stock–recruit parameters `"R0"`, `"alpha"`, and
`"beta"`. `slots` gives the cell(s) to profile (usually just the species index)
and `values` the grid of values for each; more than one slot profiles over the
full grid of combinations.

```{r}
# 1-D profile: sigmaR for species 1 (natural-scale alias)
prof_sigmaR <- profile(
  fitted = model_1,
  param    = "sigmaR",
  slots    = list(1),
  values   = list(seq(0.1, 1.5, by = 0.1))
)

plot(prof_sigmaR)   # components, with the total overlaid; see below

# 1-D profile: SRR alpha for species 1
# (alias fills in the rec_pars column; slot is just the species index)
prof_alpha <- profile(
  fitted = model_1,
  param    = "alpha",
  slots    = list(1),
  values   = list(seq(2, 80, length.out = 20))
)

# Profile M1 for species 1, sex 1, age 1
prof_M_sex <- profile(
  fitted = model_1,
  param    = "M1",
  # One slot per sex on a two-sex model. This one is single-sex, so sex 1 is
  # the only slot there is -- asking for sex 2 is out of bounds for log_M1.
  slots    = list(c(1, 1, 1)),
  values   = list(seq(0.10, 0.40, by = 0.05))
)
```

### Moving a set of cells together

`slots` cross, so *k* slots give a *k*-dimensional profile: an empirical
age-based M profiled over 13 values across ten ages would be `13^10` fits.
`joint` puts every named cell on **one** grid instead: `"multiply"` scales each
cell's current value, preserving the shape of the schedule (`1` is the fitted
model), and `"add"` shifts it, preserving the increments (`0` is the fitted
model).

```{r}
sp <- 1
prof_M_all <- profile(
  fitted = model_1,
  param  = "M1",
  slots  = lapply(seq_len(model_1$data_list$nages[sp]),
                  function(a) c(sp, 1, a)),   # every age bin of species 1
  values = list(seq(0.7, 1.3, by = 0.05)),
  joint  = "multiply"
)

plot_profile(prof_M_all)
```

### Catchability

`param = "q"` profiles a fleet's base catchability, and `slots` takes a fleet
name. Fleets sharing a `Catchability_index` share one q, so naming any member
profiles the whole group; the others are added with a message.

```{r}
prof_q <- profile(
  fitted = model_1,
  param  = "q",
  slots  = list("Bottom_trawl"),
  values = list(seq(0.5, 2.0, by = 0.1))
)
```

`profile()` returns `Rceattle_list` (one fit per grid row, `NULL` where the fit failed), `grid` (the user-scale value grid, a multiplier or offset under `joint`), `nll` (joint NLL aligned with `grid`, `NA` for non-converged fits), `alias` (the natural-scale name you profiled under, if you used one), `joint`, and echoes of `param` and `slots`. To cross-profile across species, supply one slot per species (e.g. `slots = list(1, 2, 3)` with `param = "sigmaR"`); across sex on a two-sex model with sex-specific M1 (`M1_model` 2 or 3), one slot per sex (e.g. `slots = list(c(1, 1, 1), c(1, 2, 1))` with `param = "M1"`). `cores` behaves as in the other diagnostic functions.

### Where the data disagree

The total says how well the data determine the parameter, not whether the data
sources agree about it: a smooth quadratic total can be two surveys pulling in
opposite directions. `plot_profile()` draws the components separately, as
`r4ss::SSplotProfile()` does.

```{r}
prof_M <- profile(
  fitted = model_1,
  param  = "M1",
  slots  = list(c(1, 1, 1)),
  values = list(seq(0.20, 0.45, by = 0.025))
)

plot_profile(prof_M, xlab = "M at age 1")
```

Read it by **where each curve bottoms out**, not by how deep it is: every series
is re-zeroed at its own minimum and a point marks it, so the spread of those
points along the x axis is the disagreement. The heavy black line is the total.

When one component dwarfs the rest, the others flatten onto the axis;
`relative = "scaled"` puts every curve on 0 to 1 so the minima can be compared.
It discards magnitude, so raise `minfraction` alongside it.

`profile_components()` returns the same numbers, one row per grid point per
component, each labelled with the fleet or species it belongs to.

```{r}
comps <- profile_components(prof_M)
head(comps)
```

Under `random_rec = TRUE` the total is the Laplace-approximated marginal
likelihood while the components are the inner joint negative log-likelihood, so
they will not sum; compare the shapes, not the sums. See `?plot_profile` for
`relative`, `minfraction`, model overlays, and which components `weighted = FALSE`
changes.

## Comparing runs

Overlaying sensitivity runs is itself a diagnostic: large divergences in biomass or mortality deserve scrutiny.

```{r}
mod_list  <- list(model_1, model_1_retro$Rceattle_list$Year_2019)
mod_names <- 1:length(mod_list)

plot_biomass(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names)
plot_recruitment(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names, add_ci = TRUE)
plot_ssb_depletion(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names)
```


## Collecting it into report tables

`report_tables()` gathers into tidy tables the fit, the likelihood
decomposition, the time series with uncertainty, the reference points, the fits
to index and catch, and whichever diagnostics you pass it:

```{r}
tabs <- report_tables(model_1,
                      retro = model_1_retro, jitter = jitters, osa = osa)
tabs
tabs$retrospective          # Mohn's rho by species and forecast year
tabs$osa                    # SDNR and tail statistics per fleet
```

It never refits, so a diagnostic you have not run is an absent section.
Check the `basis` column of `tabs$reference_points` before quoting a reference
point: quantities the fit never estimated are returned as `NA` with the reason.
`standard_output()` relabels the result for the `stockplotr` and `asar`
reporting packages.

## Model average

To average estimates across model variants, see `?model_average`.

```{r}
mod_avg <- model_average(list(model_1, model_1), weights = c(1,1))
plot_biomass(mod_avg)
```

With `uncertainty = TRUE`, each fit's parameters are drawn from its asymptotic
covariance. Under any harvest control rule but `"NoFishing"`, an
`estimateMode = "Estimate"` fit is refused unless it used
`fit_control(projection_uncertainty = TRUE)`, which works for fixed-effects fits
under any rule but `"ConstantF"`; `?model_average` gives the refits.
A `"Hindcast"` refit projects with no fishing, so its averaged projection is of
an unfished stock.
